title: By the River
focus: despair and renewal by the river

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha reaches the river and, sick of himself, leans to drown. From deep within comes the sacred word Om, and he falls into a deep sleep under a coconut tree. He wakes renewed; Govinda, now a monk, has watched over him without recognizing him. Siddhartha reflects that he had to experience despair to learn its emptiness, and decides to stay by the river.

vocabulary.context: Never before by sleep, he had been thus refreshed, thus renewed, thus rejuvenated!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “rejuvenated”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + ven (Latin venire, "to come") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: There, where I ran away from, there everything smelled of ointments, of spices, of wine, of excess, of sloth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ointment”: -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To forget, as what has been learned
vocabulary.context: I had to spend many years losing my spirit, to unlearn thinking again, to forget the oneness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unlearn”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors
vocabulary.context: What all agony of these recent times, all sobering realizations, all desperation had not brought about, this was brought on by this moment, when the Om entered his consciousness: he became aware of himself in his misery and in his error.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sober”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The spasmodic ejection of matter from the stomach through the mouth
vocabulary.context: This was the great vomiting he had longed for: death, the smashing to bits of the form he hated!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “vomiting”: mit (Latin mittere, "to send") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Feeling pain or sorrow on account of sins or offenses
vocabulary.context: But as a young man, I followed the penitents, lived in the forest, suffered of heat and frost, learned to hunger, taught my body to become dead.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “penitent”: -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To break in pieces by violence
vocabulary.context: This was the great vomiting he had longed for: death, the smashing to bits of the form he hated!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “smash”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To contend, by grappling with, and striving to trip or throw down, an opponent
vocabulary.context: Was this not his self, his small, frightened, and proud self, he had wrestled with for so many years, which had defeated him again and again, which was back again after every killing, prohibited joy, felt fear?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “wrestle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: I’m wearing them, because I have been a rich man, and I’m wearing my hair like the worldly and lustful people, for I have been one of them.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “lustful”: -ful (Old English -full, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To reduce to nothing or nonexistence
vocabulary.context: There was nothing left for him, except to annihilate himself, except to smash the failure into which he had shaped his life, to throw it away, before the feet of mockingly laughing gods.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “annihilate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Om is the sacred syllable in Hindu and Buddhist traditions, representing ultimate reality.

significance: Rebirth by water is a classic archetype; the river becomes the novel's central symbol.
discussionQuestions: Why does Siddhartha say he had to experience despair himself?
Where does symbolism appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the unity of all things?

items.prompt: What does Siddhartha intend to do at the river?
Who watches over him while he sleeps?
Does Govinda recognize him at first?
In the line “Never before by sleep, he had been thus refreshed, thus renewed, thus rejuvenated!”, what does “rejuvenated” most nearly mean?
options: To forget, as what has been learned
Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “By the River,” how does Hesse show despair and renewal by the river? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the symbolism you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In By the River, how does Hesse develop the idea of despair and renewal by the river? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the symbolism in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how By the River develops the idea of despair and renewal by the river. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of symbolism and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of By the River (where it begins, turns and ends) and its symbolism shape the reader's understanding of despair and renewal by the river. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what By the River suggests about despair and renewal by the river. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's symbolism and imagery), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses symbolism in By the River to complicate the reader's understanding of despair and renewal by the river. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate By the River within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of despair and renewal by the river responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read By the River alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of despair and renewal by the river follows or bends those conventions, using the symbolism as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to By the River and its treatment of despair and renewal by the river. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's symbolism and imagery, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads By the River as evidence for a larger claim about despair and renewal by the river in Siddhartha. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads By the River as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of despair and renewal by the river. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

satQuestions.passage: I had to spend many years losing my spirit, to unlearn thinking again, to forget the oneness.
satQuestions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “unlearn” most nearly mean?
options: To reduce to nothing or nonexistence
To forget, as what has been learned
To contend, by grappling with, and striving to trip or throw down, an opponent

satQuestions.passage: Siddhartha was deeply shocked. So this was how things were with him, so doomed was he, so much he had lost his way and was forsaken by all knowledge, that he had been able to seek death, that this wish, this wish of a child, had been able to grow in him: to find rest by annihilating his body! What all agony of these recent times, all sobering realizations, all desperation had not brought about, this was brought on by this moment, when the Om entered his consciousness: he became aware of himself in his misery and in his error.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “By the River”?
options: Despair and renewal by the river
The wedding night and its catastrophe

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Siddhartha say he had to experience despair himself? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are rejuvenated, ointments, unlearn, sobering, vomiting. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Never before by sleep, he had been thus refreshed, thus renewed, thus rejuvenated!” Webster's says: Rendered young again. Now the word history: “rejuvenated”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + ven (Latin venire, "to come") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “ointment”: -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “unlearn”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Om is the sacred syllable in Hindu and Buddhist traditions, representing ultimate reality. Why does this chapter matter? Rebirth by water is a classic archetype; the river becomes the novel's central symbol. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for symbolism.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see symbolism, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to despair and renewal by the river.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Symbolism, Imagery, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of symbolism. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Siddhartha was deeply shocked. So this was how things were with him, so doomed was he, so much he had lost his way and was forsaken by all knowledge, that he had been able to seek death, that this wish, this wish of a child, had been able to grow in him: to find rest by annihilating his body! What all agony of these recent times, all sobering realizations, all desperation had not brought about, this was brought on by this moment, when the Om entered his consciousness: he became aware of himself in his misery and in his error.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Symbolism, Imagery, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “By the River,” how does Hesse show despair and renewal by the river? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the symbolism you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the search for self-knowledge? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about despair and renewal by the river, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how symbolism shapes despair and renewal by the river. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
